explanation: Muku - A name derived from the fusion of "nothing" and "stain", reflecting a balance between the emptiness the Tao prizes and the spotless conduct the Fortunes reward. It is often embraced by those who strive for purity of intent without pride in it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama name list without kanji. The most conventional spelling is 無垢, mu (nothing) plus ku (dirt, stain), the ordinary word for unblemished or innocent, read in its standard on readings; an alternative is 椋, the muku tree (Aphananthe aspera), a plant name of the kind Edo commoners bore. A commoner name.

name: Chiki
explanation: Chiki - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the tea ceremony, in which a single bowl is served with a thousand small courtesies, this name represents a thousand joys gathered into one quiet hour. It is often chosen by those who appreciate stillness and exactness and have a deep respect for the tea masters who make a lifetime of practice look effortless.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. The conventional kanji are 千喜, chi (thousand) plus ki (joy), both in standard readings. A commoner register name of the two-character auspicious type.

name: Mutsu
explanation: The name Mutsu is associated with the famous Accord of the Six Villages, in which six feuding hamlets along one river agreed under a magistrate's seal to share their irrigation water by turns rather than by force. Those who choose this name try to embody values of harmony, neighborly good faith and the patience to settle a quarrel by talking.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 睦, mutsu (harmony, friendly intimacy, as in mutsumajii), a standard kun reading; the name is unrelated to Mutsu province (陸奥), which uses different characters. A commoner register name. Modern association: the battleship Mutsu and the Mutsu region of northern Japan, both from the province name rather than this kanji.

name: Yoso
explanation: The name Yoso is inspired by the far frontier villages beyond the last post-station, known for their hard winters and for taking in whoever arrives on the road. The name reflects the openness of such distant places and is often chosen by those who value hospitality to strangers and a willingness to leave home for a new beginning.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. There is no fixed kanji; the sound is the common word yoso (elsewhere, another place, written 余所 or 他所), which the explanation draws on, and register names of this shape were usually written phonetically, e.g. 与曽 (give, formerly) as ateji with no meaning of its own. A commoner register name.

name: Urako
explanation: Urako - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Returning Boats, an event that emphasizes the gratitude of a fishing bay for every hull that comes home from the autumn storms. People choose this name to reflect their values for shelter, homecoming and the quiet safety of a harbor after open water.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: appears in a Nanbokucho-period list of court women with the kanji 浦子, ura (bay, inlet, seashore) plus ko (child); the on reading would be Hoshi, the kun reading Urako. A court name of the medieval -ko type. Not to be confused with the common noun urako (an unrelated modern usage is rare).

name: Tsugi
explanation: Tsugi - This name signifies the unbroken succession of a household from one generation to the next, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values continuity, duty to ancestors and the quiet work of keeping a line alive.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1774 Noshio), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 継, tsugi (to succeed, to carry on, as in ato-tsugi, an heir), a standard kun reading; 次 (next) is an equally plausible spelling for a daughter born after another child. A commoner register name.

name: Hata
explanation: Hata chose her name in honor of the famous Crane weaver Asahina Hata, who wove a single bolt of silk so fine that the daimyo hung it in place of a painted screen and made her the first commoner ever named a treasure of the province.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1774 Noshio), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 機, hata (a loom, as in hata-ori, weaving), a standard kun reading; 旗 (banner) is the other common spelling of the same sound. A commoner register name of the object type. The Asahina weaver in the explanation is invented, and the sound also matches the historical Hata (秦) immigrant clan of ancient Japan, which is unrelated.

name: Noe
explanation: Noe - Composed of the elements "no" (open field) and "e" (river inlet), this name symbolizes the fertile ground where flat farmland meets slow water. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of plenty, rootedness and a village that has always had enough to eat.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1809 Kamikiyoto), written in historical kana as のゑ with the old character we (ゑ), read Noe. The conventional kanji are 野江, no (field) plus e (inlet, river branch), both standard kun readings; 乃恵 (blessing) is a common alternative. A commoner register name.

name: Kima
explanation: Kima - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Honest Seamstress, in which a village girl found a purse of gold in a torn sleeve she was mending and walked three days to return it to its owner, who was so moved that he adopted her as his heir. It reflects qualities such as honesty, joy in plain work and trust in the Fortunes to reward the right thing.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1690 Goromaru), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji are 喜真, ki (joy) plus ma (truth, genuine), both standard readings; the register spelling gives no kanji, so this is a plausible reconstruction rather than a recorded one. A commoner register name. The tale in the explanation is invented.

name: Tsuyo
explanation: Tsuyo - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The reed that bends in the flood is stronger than the oak that is broken by it", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value endurance, resilience and the strength to outlast trouble rather than to fight it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1733 Hatcho), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 強, tsuyo (strong, the stem of tsuyoi), a standard kun reading. A commoner register name of the virtue-word type, the female counterpart of names like Take. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani rendering of a familiar East Asian saying, not a specific historical text.

name: Mare
explanation: Mare - With origins in the legend of the Once-Born Crane, a bird said to appear only once in a hundred years over a village that would prosper, this name evokes a sense of rarity, wonder and being singled out by the heavens. It appeals to those who admire the extraordinary and believe their daughter was a gift not to be expected twice.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 稀, mare (rare, uncommon), a standard kun reading; 希 is a common alternative. A commoner register name, often given to a child born late or after long waiting. The legend in the explanation is invented.

name: Gonko
explanation: Gonko - Stemming from the word "gon", which denotes authority and the right to act in another's name, this name embodies the spirit of a woman trusted to speak for her house. It resonates with those who are capable, discreet and comfortable holding power on behalf of someone else.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: appears in a Nanbokucho-period list of court women with the kanji 權子, the old form of 権 (authority, power; also provisional or acting, as in the office title gon-no-kami) plus 子 (child); the on reading is Gonshi, with Gonko the kun-style reading given here. A court name of the medieval -ko type. Rare in modern Japan and with no notable modern bearer.

name: Fukuju
explanation: Fukuju - This name is inspired by the natural element of the fukuju-so, the golden flower that opens through the last snow at the turn of the year, symbolizing good fortune and long life arriving together. It is often chosen for its connection to the New Year and its representation of prosperity, endurance and hope that outlasts the winter.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in a Nanbokucho-period list of commoner women as 福寿女, fuku (good fortune) plus ju (long life) with the suffix 女 (woman), a marker medieval records attached to female commoners' names; the given name proper is Fukuju, both characters in standard on readings. A commoner name of the auspicious-word type, and the word fukuju also names the New Year flower Adonis ramosa, which the explanation uses.

name: Konabe
explanation: Konabe - A name derived from the fusion of "small" and "cooking pot", reflecting a balance between humility and the daily nourishment that keeps a household alive. It is often embraced by those who strive for usefulness and warmth rather than grandeur.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama name list without kanji. The conventional spelling is 小鍋, ko (small) plus nabe (pot, pan), both standard kun readings; household-object names of this kind were genuinely borne by women of the period. A commoner name.

name: Run
explanation: Run - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of lacquerware, in which coat after coat is laid down and left to stay until the surface holds for a hundred years, this name represents what remains when patience is finished. It is often chosen by those who appreciate durability over show and have a deep respect for the craftsmen who let time do half the work.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list and in an Edo village register (1804 Nishitomioka), recorded in kana as るん. There is no conventional kanji: names ending in n were written phonetically, most often 留ん, ru (to stay, to remain) plus the kana n, and the explanation draws on that character; the reading is therefore partly kana and should be flagged as unusual. A commoner register name.

name: Junko
explanation: The name Junko is associated with the famous Submission of the Seven Lords, in which seven provincial daimyo who had defied the throne laid down their swords before the Emperor rather than see their domains burn. Those who choose this name try to embody values of obedience, gentleness in victory and loyalty that puts the Empire above pride.
notes: Court name following the attested Heian pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子: 順子 was borne by Fujiwara no Junshi (Nobuko, 809-871), consort of Emperor Ninmyo, and Junko is the kun-style reading of the same characters, with Junshi the on reading. The kanji are 順 (obedient, gentle, in due order) and 子 (child). A court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: Junko is one of the most common twentieth-century Japanese female names, so it reads as familiar rather than archaic.

name: Rinko
explanation: The name Rinko is inspired by the Hall of Right Conduct, a magistrates' academy in a river town known for training clerks who cannot be bribed. The name reflects the moral order of the place and is often chosen by those who value ethics, propriety and the correct relations between lord and retainer, parent and child.
notes: Court name following the attested Heian pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子: 倫子 was borne by Minamoto no Rinshi (964-1053), the principal wife of Fujiwara no Michinaga, and Rinko is the kun-style reading of the same characters, with Rinshi the on reading. The kanji are 倫 (ethics, morals, proper human relations) and 子 (child). A court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Hagi
explanation: Hagi - This name pays tribute to the Viewing of the Seven Autumn Grasses, an event that emphasizes the bittersweet beauty of the year's decline as families walk the field margins to admire the bush clover in bloom. People choose this name to reflect their values for gentleness, the grace of small things and an acceptance of the seasons' turning.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of the plant names Edo commoners bore, alongside Kiku, Matsu and Ume. The kanji is 萩, hagi (bush clover, Lespedeza), a standard kun reading and the first of the traditional seven autumn grasses. A commoner-style name. Hagi is also the name of a castle town in western Japan, unrelated.

name: Hibari
explanation: Hibari - This name means "skylark". It represents the small bird that climbs straight up out of a spring field and sings from the top of the sky, a symbol of cheerfulness, effort and a voice that carries farther than its size.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of the animal and plant names borne by Edo commoners, like Tsuru (crane) and Kame (tortoise). The kanji are 雲雀, literally cloud-sparrow, read as a single word hibari - a jukujikun reading in which the characters give the meaning and not the sound, so it should be flagged as stylized. A commoner-style name. Modern association: the singer Misora Hibari, the most famous Japanese entertainer of the postwar era.

name: Hotaru
explanation: Hotaru - This name signifies the firefly that lights the summer marsh for a single season, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values a brief but brilliant life, the beauty of the sixth-month evenings and light that comes from within.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of the animal and plant names Edo commoners bore. The kanji is 蛍, hotaru (firefly), a standard kun reading. A commoner-style name. Modern association: the character Tomoe Hotaru in Sailor Moon, and the firefly-viewing season in general.

name: Uta
explanation: Uta - A name that means "song", evoking the poems sung at festivals, the planting songs of the paddies and a voice that lifts everyone within hearing.
notes: Not in the tagged registers for this batch but a genuine Edo commoner name (うた appears in period registers elsewhere), so it is kept as an attested rather than invented entry. The conventional kanji is 歌, uta (song, poem), a standard kun reading; 詩 (poem) is an alternative. A commoner register name of the single-word type. Modern association: still a common given name, and the sound is the same as in waka poetry.

name: Wasa
explanation: Wasa chose her name in honor of the famous Crane courtier Doji Wasa, who ended a year-long dispute between two great houses by seating their lords at one tea gathering and refusing to let either leave before the other had bowed.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of the two-mora kana names of Edo village registers, and the sound わさ does occur as a commoner name in the period, so it may well be attested elsewhere. The conventional kanji are 和佐, wa (harmony, peace) plus sa (to assist), both standard readings, though such names were usually written phonetically. A commoner-style name; the Doji Wasa of the explanation is invented.

name: Zenko
explanation: Zenko was a deity that was said to have taught the first villagers to share their harvest after she saw a mother give her own bowl to a stranger's child.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of an auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 善子: 善 'goodness, virtue' (zen, the on reading) + 子 'child' (ko); the Heian scholarly convention would read it Zenshi, so Zenko mixes an on reading with kun ko, which is common in later usage. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Zuiko
explanation: Zuiko - Derived from the phrase "a sign of good fortune", this name embodies the idea of a child who arrives as a blessing already foretold. It is often associated with those who are born under a favorable omen or into a season of plenty.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of an auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 瑞子: 瑞 'auspicious omen, felicitous sign' (zui, on reading) + 子 'child' (ko); Heian court convention would read it Zuishi. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Jueiko
explanation: Jueiko - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A long life is the root, and honor is the flower", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value endurance first and glory only as its natural fruit.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of two auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 寿栄子: 寿 'longevity, long life' (ju) + 栄 'glory, flourishing' (ei) + 子 'child' (ko), all on readings except ko; a three-kanji -ko name is rarer than the two-kanji form and the reading is somewhat stylized. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Eijuko
explanation: Eijuko - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the longevity dance performed at New Year, this name represents the wish for a glorious life that endures. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the slow, deliberate grace of the old dances and have a deep respect for the elders who still perform them.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of two auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 栄寿子: 栄 'glory, flourishing' (ei) + 寿 'longevity' (ju) + 子 'child' (ko), on readings except ko; a three-kanji -ko name is rarer than the two-kanji form and the reading is somewhat stylized. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Mitsuko
explanation: Mitsuko chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Mitsuko, who lit the lanterns of a besieged castle every night for a winter so that its garrison would never believe itself forgotten by the Emperor.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Mitsuko 光子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Koshi). Kanji 光子: 光 (mitsu, light, radiance) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: in physics 光子 read koshi is the word for photon, a coincidence that is occasionally the subject of jokes about the name.

name: Ritsu
explanation: The name Ritsu is inspired by the Hall of Ordinances in the Imperial City, known for its rows of lacquered cabinets where every edict of the Emperor is copied and kept. The name reflects the orderliness of the place and is often chosen by those who value discipline, exactness and a life kept in measure.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo village registers (1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka), where it was recorded in kana as りつ. The conventional kanji is 律 (ritsu, "law, rule, measure", also the word for a musical mode), read with its ordinary on-reading. A commoner register name for women, not a court -ko form. In modern Japan Ritsu is a unisex given name and is familiar from the manga and anime K-On! (Tainaka Ritsu).

name: Joko
explanation: The name Joko is inspired by the Springs of the Unclouded Pool, a mountain shrine in Dragon lands known for its icy water that is said to have never once run muddy. The name reflects the purity of the place and is often chosen by those who value clean hands, honest speech and a heart with nothing hidden in it.
notes: Not recorded on any historical person in our sources; the name is built on the attested Heian and Kamakura court pattern of an auspicious kanji plus 子, and is plausible under that pattern even though we have no record of a specific bearer named Joko. Written 浄子: 浄 (jō, "pure, clean") plus 子 (ko, "child"), read with the on-reading of 浄 as court -ko names usually were. A court-style name in this setting, though -ko may be borne by any caste. No notable modern association; 浄 is common in Buddhist vocabulary (as in Jōdo, the Pure Land).

name: Wakiko
explanation: Wakiko chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Wakiko, who settled a blood feud between two Crane vassal houses by hosting both at a single tea gathering and refusing to let either leave until they had drunk from the same bowl.
notes: Not recorded on any historical person in our sources; the name follows the attested Heian court pattern of auspicious kanji plus 子 and is plausible under it, but we have no record of a specific historical Wakiko. Written 和貴子: 和 (wa, "harmony, peace"), 貴 (ki, "noble, precious") and 子 (ko, "child"). The three-kanji shape is slightly fuller than the usual two-kanji court name but each reading is standard. A court-style name in this setting; -ko is acceptable for any caste. No notable modern association.

name: Kou
explanation: Kou - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Good fortune enters the house that sweeps its own doorstep", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value diligence, gratitude and the quiet luck that follows an orderly life.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama period name list and in the 1837 Matsushima village register, recorded in kana as こう. The conventional kanji is 幸 (kō, "good fortune, happiness"); other spellings such as 香 ("fragrance") were also used for this sound, so the register gives no way to choose between them. A commoner register name for women, not a court -ko form. In modern Japan the name is more familiar in its extended forms (Kōko, Kōichi); Kou itself is now rare.

name: Bara
explanation: Bara - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Thorned Gift, in which a peasant girl carried a wild rose through a Winter Court to a Crane lady and was rewarded not for the flower but for the unscratched patience with which she carried it. It reflects qualities such as endurance, care and beauty guarded by thorns.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a plant name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it. 薔薇 (bara, rose) is the conventional spelling; both kanji are used only for this word, so the reading is fixed. Commoner register style, not a court name. The rose was not a favored flower in pre-modern Japan, so as a name it is a deliberate oddity rather than a period-typical choice.

name: Benka
explanation: Benka - With origins in the legend of the dyer Benka, who is said to have coaxed the first true crimson out of safflower petals for an Empress's robe, this name evokes a sense of craft, patience and vivid color. It appeals to those who admire the quiet artisans whose work is worn by the great.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a plant name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it. 紅花 (safflower) is normally read benibana; Benka is a stylized on-reading of both kanji and would be read that way only if the surrounding prose explains it. Commoner register style, not a court name. The safflower was the source of the red dye beni, which links the name to the dye trade.

name: Beniko
explanation: Beniko - Stemming from the word "beni", which denotes the crimson dye pressed from safflower petals, this name embodies the spirit of vivid, unfading color. It resonates with those who are striking, warm and unwilling to fade into a crowd.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (an auspicious kanji + 子 ko, the Heian court pattern); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 紅 (beni, crimson) + 子 (ko, child) reads Beniko without difficulty. A -ko name in the court style, acceptable for any caste in this setting. Beniko is a real but uncommon modern given name.

name: Benie
explanation: Benie - This name is inspired by the natural element of the crimson inlet, where the water reddens at sunset, symbolizing warmth held in a sheltered place. It is often chosen for its connection to quiet harbors and its representation of beauty that does not need to be announced.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 紅 (beni, crimson) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Benie straightforwardly. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Wakae
explanation: Wakae - A name derived from the fusion of "young" and "inlet", reflecting a balance between fresh vigor and the stillness of sheltered water. It is often embraced by those who strive for youthful energy kept within calm bounds.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 若 (waka, young) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Wakae without difficulty. Commoner register style, not a court name. Wakae is better known as a place name (Wakae in Osaka, site of a Sengoku-era castle) and a surname than as a given name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Wano
explanation: Wano - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Mended Fences, an event that emphasizes settling old quarrels between neighbors before the planting season. People choose this name to reflect their values for harmony, reconciliation and the peace of a village that works together.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 乃 no, which Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 和 (wa, harmony) + 乃 (no, possessive particle) reads Wano straightforwardly. Commoner register style, not a court name. Wano is also the name of a fictional country in the manga One Piece, spelled differently. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Wakano
explanation: Wakano - This name means "of youth". It represents the freshness and promise of a life still early in its course, and the hope that its bearer keeps that freshness as she ages.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 乃 no, which Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 若 (waka, young) + 乃 (no, possessive particle) reads Wakano without difficulty. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Goma
explanation: Goma means "sesame" or "small seed", which can suggest a humble crop that yields rich oil or something tiny that becomes precious once pressed. People with this name may be modest in appearance but generous in what they give.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a plant name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it. 胡麻 (goma, sesame) is the standard spelling and reading. Commoner register style, not a court name. In modern usage goma is mostly the food word, and goma-suri (grinding sesame) is slang for flattery.

name: Zusa
explanation: Zusa can be written with two different kanji. One means "auspicious help", and the other means "auspicious sand". The choice of kanji could reflect what the parents hoped for, such as a daughter who would be a support to the household or one whose good fortune would be as plentiful as grains on a shore.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (auspicious kanji combined as a two-character name, the pattern behind court and samurai women's names); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 瑞 (zui, auspicious) + 佐 (sa, help) gives Zusa only by clipping the first element to zu-, a stylized reading that should be explained in surrounding prose; the alternative in the explanation is 瑞沙 (sand). Commoner register style, not a court name.

name: Zuie
explanation: Zuie - A name that means "auspicious inlet", evoking a sheltered bay where good omens gather like boats coming home.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 瑞 (zui, auspicious) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Zuie. Caution: the same two kanji as a place name (Mizue in Tokyo's Edogawa ward) are read Mizue, so Zuie is the on-reading and may need explaining. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Enomi
explanation: Enomi - Derived from the phrase "a blessing borne as fruit", this name embodies the idea of grace that ripens into something one can hold and share. It is often associated with those who turn good fortune into good works.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - an auspicious compound of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it. 恵 (e, blessing) + 実 (mi, fruit) yields E-mi; the -no- is an inserted connective, so Enomi is a stylized reading that surrounding prose should explain. Commoner register style, not a court name.

name: Ranno
explanation: Ranno - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Orchid in the Ravine, in which a flower bloomed unseen for a hundred years until a lost monk found it and understood that virtue needs no witness. It reflects qualities such as refinement, patience and integrity without audience.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 乃 no, which Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 蘭 (ran, orchid) + 乃 (no, possessive particle) reads Ranno. Commoner register style, not a court name. The orchid is one of the Four Gentlemen of Chinese painting, which gives the name a scholarly overtone. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Chigusa
explanation: Chigusa - Stemming from the word "chigusa", which denotes a thousand grasses, the full green of a summer meadow, this name embodies the spirit of abundance and variety. It resonates with those who are many-sided, restless and full of life.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a plant name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it as a pre-modern given name. 千 (chi, thousand) + 草 (kusa/gusa, grass) reads Chigusa naturally and is also a poetic word for a meadow. Commoner register style, not a court name. Chigusa is a real modern given name and a surname.

name: Chidori
explanation: Chidori - This name is inspired by the natural element of the plover, the small shore bird that runs in zigzags along the tide line, symbolizing lightness and the endurance of small things against wind and wave. It is often chosen for its connection to the winter shore and its representation of playful resilience.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a bird name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it as a given name. 千 (chi, thousand) + 鳥 (tori/dori, bird) reads Chidori and is the ordinary word for a plover; it is also a classic textile and lacquer motif. Commoner register style, not a court name. Chidori is a familiar modern word (the chidori check pattern, Chidorigafuchi in Tokyo) and the name of a lightning technique in the manga Naruto.

name: Futaba
explanation: Futaba - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of bonsai, this name represents the first pair of leaves a seedling opens, from which a master reads the tree it will become. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patient shaping over years and have a deep respect for gardeners who see the grown tree in the sprout.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a plant name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it as a pre-modern given name. 双 (futa, pair) + 葉 (ha/ba, leaf) reads Futaba and is the ordinary word for a seedling's first two leaves; the proverb sendan wa futaba yori kanbashi (the sandalwood is fragrant from its first leaves) uses it. Commoner register style, not a court name. Futaba is a common modern given name and place name.

name: Itoe
explanation: The name Itoe is associated with the famous Weaving of the Flood Nets, in which the women of a river town spun every thread they owned into nets that held back the driftwood of a great flood. Those who choose this name try to embody values of cooperation, practical devotion and strength made from many small strands.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 糸 (ito, thread) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Itoe. Ito on its own is a well attested Edo commoner name, which makes this a natural extension. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Nazuna
explanation: Nazuna can be written with two different kanji. One means "shepherd's purse", the humble spring herb of the Seven Herbs, and the other means "vegetable and sand", a phonetic spelling. The choice of kanji could reflect the family's circumstances, such as a farm household naming a daughter for the weed that feeds them in lean months or a townsfolk family choosing pretty characters for the sound.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - a plant name of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it as a pre-modern given name. 薺 (nazuna, shepherd's purse) is the single standard kanji and reading; the phonetic alternative in the explanation is 菜砂. Commoner register style, not a court name. Nazuna has become a moderately popular modern given name.

name: Nene
explanation: Nene - This name signifies peace doubled, calm repeated until it becomes a habit, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values tranquility, steadiness and a home without shouting.
notes: Marked invented in our metadata, but in honesty the name is attested: Nene was the name of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's principal wife (Kita no Mandokoro, late Sengoku), and a two-mora doubled name of this shape is exactly the kind Edo commoner women bore. 寧 (nei/ne, peace) with the repetition mark 々 gives Nene; the kanji spelling is a later convention, since her name was written in kana. Commoner register style, not a court name. Nene is a well known historical figure in Japan, so the name carries that association.

name: Nobue
explanation: Nobue - A name that means "inlet of trust", evoking a harbor whose water can always be relied on to be calm.

Commoner register style, not a court name. Nobue is a real, fairly common modern given name among women born in the Showa era. name: Fukino
explanation: Fukino was a deity that was said to have pushed the first green shoots through the snow crust for a starving hamlet after its children left rice cakes at her frozen spring.

name: Fujie
explanation: Fujie - Derived from the phrase "wisteria over the inlet", this name embodies the idea of grace that hangs above still water. It is often associated with those who are gentle, ornamental in the best sense, and rooted more deeply than they look.

name: Ineno
explanation: Ineno - Composed of the elements "rice plant" and "of", this name symbolizes belonging to the crop that feeds the Empire. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of plenty, humility and a farm household's pride in its harvest.

name: Ikue
explanation: Ikue - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Countless Inlets, in which a fisherman's daughter was told to count every cove on her coast and, finding them beyond number, learned instead to know each by name. It reflects qualities such as patience, attentiveness and love for one's home ground.
