(Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Juyo
explanation: Juyo - With origins in the legend of the crone Juyo, who outlived seven Emperors and was consulted by the eighth on what the first had been like, this name evokes a sense of longevity and living memory. It appeals to those who admire elders who carry the past forward for the young.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 代 yo, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 寿 (ju, longevity) + 代 (yo, generation) reads Juyo, though pairing the on-reading ju with the kun-reading yo is a mixed reading that may need explaining. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Jinae
explanation: Jinae - Stemming from the word "jin", which denotes benevolence, the first of the Confucian virtues, this name embodies the spirit of compassion given a place to rest. It resonates with those who are kind by principle rather than by mood.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 仁 (jin, benevolence) + 江 (e, inlet) yields Jin-e; the -a- is an inserted connective, so Jinae is a stylized reading that surrounding prose should explain. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Jakue
explanation: Jakue - This name is inspired by the natural element of the still inlet at dawn, before any boat has moved, symbolizing silence that is full rather than empty. It is often chosen for its connection to quiet water and its representation of the calm the Tao prizes above noise.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 寂 (jaku, stillness, the Buddhist quiet of nirvana) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Jakue; jaku is an on-reading with a monastic flavor, so the name leans religious. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Rokuno
explanation: Rokuno - A name derived from the fusion of "six" and "of", reflecting a balance between the fixed order of number and the openness of belonging. It is often embraced by those who strive for their place in a large family, being sixth-born or sixth-blessed.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 乃 no, which Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 六 (roku, six) + 乃 (no, possessive particle) reads Rokuno. Number names for children by birth order are well attested among Edo commoners, which supports the pattern. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Uzue
explanation: The name Uzue is associated with the famous Whirlpool Straits Crossing, in which a fleet was lost to the tide and the one boatwoman who read the eddies brought her passengers through alive. Those who choose this name try to embody values of nerve, local knowledge and respect for the sea's moods.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 渦 (uzu, eddy) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Uzue. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Eiri
explanation: Eiri - This name represents glory governed by reason and is often chosen by those who are ambitious for their household or who are expected to win advancement without losing their judgment.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (auspicious kanji combined as a two-character name, the pattern behind court and samurai women's names); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 栄 (ei, glory) + 理 (ri, reason) reads Eiri using on-readings. Commoner register style, not a court name. Eiri is a real but uncommon modern given name for both sexes.

name: Yasue
explanation: Yasue - This name signifies a peaceful inlet, sheltered water where nothing need be feared, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values security, ease and a household at rest.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 安 (yasu, peace) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Yasue. Commoner register style, not a court name. Yasue is a real modern given name, common among women born in the early Showa era. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Genge
explanation: The name Genge is inspired by the paddy country of the southern river plains, known for its spring fields that turn violet with milk-vetch blossom before the rice goes in. The name reflects the humble abundance of the place and is often chosen by those who value patience, quiet renewal and the work that feeds others.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant names of the kind Edo commoner women bore (registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Ine), and we have no record of Genge as a personal name. Kanji 蓮華 (lotus flower, here the milk-vetch or renge-so that carpets fallow paddies); the standard reading of 蓮華 is 'renge', and 'genge' is a regional folk name for the plant, so this is a stylized reading. Commoner register style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Zakuro
explanation: Zakuro - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Split Fruit, a late-summer village event that emphasizes fertility, abundance and the many children of a household. People choose this name to reflect their values for a full house, generosity with the harvest and the hope of a long line of descendants.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant and fruit names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Zakuro as a personal name. Kanji 石榴 (pomegranate), read 'zakuro'; the reading is the ordinary word for the fruit rather than a character-by-character reading, which is normal for this plant name. The pomegranate is a traditional emblem of fertility and of the goddess Kishimojin. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Bekko
explanation: Bekko - Composed of the elements "turtle" and "shell", this name symbolizes long life and a hard outer surface over a patient heart. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of endurance, protection and the amber warmth of a fine comb.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of object names of the kind Edo commoner women bore (registers carry Nabe pot, Kama kettle), and we have no record of Bekko as a personal name. Kanji 鼈甲 (鼈 soft-shelled turtle + 甲 shell), read 'bekko', the ordinary word for tortoiseshell as used in combs and hairpins. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Benibana
explanation: Benibana - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The dye is drawn from a thousand flowers for one length of silk", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value patient labor, the beauty that comes of many small efforts, and the worth hidden in plain things.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Benibana as a personal name. Kanji 紅花 (紅 crimson + 花 flower), read 'benibana', the safflower whose petals gave the red dye and rouge of the Edo period. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Warabi
explanation: Warabi - This name pays tribute to the Bracken Gathering, a spring calendar event in the hill villages that emphasizes the first foraging of the year, sharing the wild harvest and the hunger that ends when the snow melts. People choose this name to reflect their values for hardiness, thrift and gratitude for what the hillside gives.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant names of the kind Edo commoner women bore (registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Ine), and we have no record of Warabi as a personal name. Kanji 蕨 (bracken fern), read 'warabi', a spring mountain vegetable and a source of starch in lean years. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Asagao
explanation: Asagao means "morning glory" or "morning face", which can suggest a bloom that opens with the dawn or a countenance that is fresh and bright at the start of each day. People with this name may be early risers, cheerful and briefly brilliant, with an appreciation for beauty that does not last.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of flower names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Asagao as a personal name, though the plant was a hugely popular Edo cultivar. Kanji 朝顔 (朝 morning + 顔 face), read 'asagao', the ordinary word for the morning glory. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting. Asagao is also the name of a chapter and a lady in The Tale of Genji.

name: Akebi
explanation: Akebi - This name signifies the sweet fruit that splits open of its own accord when ripe, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values patience, sweetness revealed in due time, and gifts that come unforced from the mountainside.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant and fruit names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Akebi as a personal name. Kanji 通草 (通 pass through + 草 grass), read 'akebi' as a whole-word reading (jukujikun) that does not follow the individual characters; 木通 is an equally common spelling. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Chiyome
explanation: Chiyome chose her name in honor of the famous Scorpion Chiyome, who gathered the widows and orphans of a border war and trained them as the eyes and ears of her lord, so that no rumor crossed the province without her hearing it.
notes: Partly attested: Chiyome is the name of Mochizuki Chiyome (望月千代女), the semi-legendary Sengoku-period woman said to have trained female agents for the Takeda, though her historicity is disputed and the name is otherwise not in our sources; it is constructed in the -me (女, woman) idiom of pre-modern female names such as Iwame or Tatsume. Kanji 千代女 (千 thousand + 代 generation, age + 女 woman), read 'chiyome', a regular reading. Fine for any caste in this setting. Modern readers may know Mochizuki Chiyome from ninja fiction and games.

name: Hozuki
explanation: Hozuki was a deity that was said to have hung lanterns of red fruit along the road of the dead after the first ancestors lost their way home at the Bon festival.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Hozuki as a personal name. Kanji 鬼灯 (鬼 demon, ghost + 灯 lamp), read 'hozuki' as a whole-word reading (jukujikun) for the ground cherry or Chinese lantern plant, whose papery red husks are set out at Bon to guide the spirits; 酸漿 is the other common spelling. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting. Modern readers may know the name from the manga Hozuki's Coolheadedness.

name: Hiiragi
explanation: Hiiragi - Derived from the phrase "holly at the gate turns the demon away", this name embodies the idea of a small, spined guardian that keeps evil from the threshold. It is often associated with those who protect their households quietly and unbendingly.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Hiiragi as a personal name; it is attested as a Japanese surname. Kanji 柊 (holly olive, the winter tree radical plus 冬 winter), read 'hiiragi', a regular reading. The sprig is hung at doorways at Setsubun with a sardine head to ward off oni. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Uguisu
explanation: Uguisu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Warbler's Cottage, in which a woodcutter is welcomed into a hidden house by a gentle woman, breaks his promise not to open the inner door, and finds only an empty plum grove and a warbler singing where the house had stood. It reflects qualities such as sweetness of voice, modesty and the sorrow of a trust betrayed.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of bird and nature names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Uguisu as a personal name. Kanji 鶯 (bush warbler), read 'uguisu', a regular reading; the bird is the classical herald of spring paired with plum blossom. The tale summarized is a genuine folktale, Uguisu no Sato. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Unohana
explanation: Unohana - Rooted in the ancient proverb "When the deutzia blooms, the cuckoo calls", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value doing things in their proper season, modest white beauty and the pairing of one good thing with another.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of flower names of the kind Edo commoner women bore, and we have no record of Unohana as a personal name. Kanji 卯の花 (卯 fourth month, the rabbit sign + の + 花 flower), read 'unohana', the deutzia that flowers in the fourth lunar month; the same word names the okara dish. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting. Unohana is the name of a captain in the manga Bleach.

name: Yomogi
explanation: Yomogi - With origins in the legend of the Herb-Woman of the Marsh, who burned mugwort on the wounds of a routed army and brought every man back to his village alive, this name evokes a sense of healing, hardiness and humble usefulness. It appeals to those who admire quiet competence over glory.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of plant names of the kind Edo commoner women bore (registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Ine), and we have no record of Yomogi as a personal name. Kanji 蓬 (mugwort), read 'yomogi', a regular reading; the plant is the moxa of moxibustion and the green of kusa-mochi. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Eika
explanation: Eika was a deity that was said to have crowned a ruined village with a single season of impossible prosperity after its headwoman gave the shrine her last measure of rice.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom as an invented name - an auspicious word of the kind Edo commoner women bore (like the register names Kiku, Matsu, Nabe), with no attested mechanism behind this specific form and no record of it as a pre-modern given name. 栄華 (ei, glory + ka, splendor) is the ordinary word eika, glory or splendor, and reads naturally. Commoner register style, not a court name. Eika is a real but uncommon modern given name.

name: Rurie
explanation: Rurie - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of cloisonne enamel, this name represents the deep lapis blue that fills the wire cells of a finished piece. It is often chosen by those who appreciate color that seems to glow from within and have a deep respect for craftsmen who fire a surface a dozen times to reach it.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 瑠璃 (ruri, lapis lazuli) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Rurie. Ruri is one of the seven treasures of Buddhist scripture, which gives it an auspicious ring. Commoner register style, not a court name. (Reclassified 2026-08-26: the stem-plus-suffix form is only weakly attested pre-modern, so this counts as an invented name under the pool's 60/30/10 rule.)

name: Wakasa
explanation: Wakasa - With origins in the legend of Lady Wakasa, a coastal governor's daughter who rowed out alone to guide a storm-scattered fishing fleet home by lantern, this name evokes a sense of youthful daring and steady nerve. It appeals to those who admire courage that serves others rather than itself.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Wakasa (b. 1527), daughter of Yaita Kiyosada of Tanegashima, on Japanese Wikipedia; a province name used as a given name, which Sengoku samurai families did for daughters. Kanji 若狭 (young + narrow), read wakasa as the province is; as a name the sense is simply the place, not the characters. Samurai-daughter style, given in kanji; no commoner register attestation.

name: Gyokuran
explanation: The name Gyokuran is associated with the famous Night of the Jade Tide, in which a spring flood that should have drowned a river town instead carried a shrine's jade offering-stone gently onto the magistrate's steps, and the town was spared. Those who choose this name try to embody values of calm before overwhelming force and trust that the Fortunes reward a household that keeps faith.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Ike Gyokuran (1727-1784), late-Edo painter and poet, on English Wikipedia; this is an art name (go), not a birth name, which is the register it belongs to. Kanji 玉瀾 (jewel + billowing waves), on-yomi gyoku + ran, a conventional literary compound. Elite or artistic style rather than a commoner register name; suits a Crane or Phoenix artist's chosen name. Gyokuran is remembered today as one of the few celebrated woman painters of the bunjin school.

name: Chacha
explanation: Chacha - This name means "tea, tea". It represents the warmth of a household where the kettle is always on, and the quiet hospitality that makes even a poor house a place guests remember.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Chacha, wife of Shima Sakon (Sengoku), on Japanese Wikipedia; the same name was borne by the far more famous Yodo-dono, Hideyoshi's concubine, in childhood. Kanji 茶々 (tea + the repetition mark), read cha-cha, a doubled pet-name form common for elite girls. Samurai-daughter or court pet-name style; not a commoner register name in our sources. Modern readers know it from Yodo-dono in every Sengoku drama.

name: Chino
explanation: Chino - Composed of the elements "a thousand" and "of", this name symbolizes belonging to something vast, a single child counted among a thousand blessings. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of humility and quiet plenty.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name, but secondhand: cited in an online thread discussing Owaki Hidekazu's Onna no shimei tanjo (Chikuma 2024) as a period commoner name that reads as modern; verify against the book before weighting it heavily. The source gives kana ちの; the conventional kanji spelling is 千乃 (thousand + the possessive particle no used as a name-ender), read chi-no without strain. Commoner register style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Chiyozuru
explanation: Chiyozuru - A name derived from the fusion of "a thousand generations" and "crane", reflecting a balance between the long patience of a lineage and the grace of a single life within it. It is often embraced by those who strive for a legacy that outlasts them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Chiyozuru, a Kamakura-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 千代鶴 (thousand + generation + crane), read chi-yo-zuru with the usual voicing of tsuru in compound; both halves are stock auspicious elements. Elite or samurai-daughter style in this period; the crane element also appears in Edo commoner registers as Tsuru.

name: Hori
explanation: Hori - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of garden-making, this name represents the moat or channel that a master cuts to bring living water through stone and moss. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the patient shaping of a landscape and have a deep respect for gardeners who make water seem to have always flowed where it flows.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Horibe Hori (b. 1675), samurai daughter of the Ako domain, on Japanese Wikipedia; the source records the name in kana ほり. Conventional kanji 堀 (moat, dug channel), read hori, kun reading; as a girl's name it is an everyday word used as a name, which was normal. Samurai-daughter style here, though the plain-word form is indistinguishable from a commoner register name.

name: Hite
explanation: The name Hite is inspired by the terraces of the eastern hill country, known for their fields that catch the first light before the valley wakes. The name reflects the bright, early-rising character of the place and is often chosen by those who value diligence and a clear head at dawn.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: recorded once among the 112 women who took refuge at the Mantokuji divorce temple in Kozuke (Ueno Kazuo et al., Namae to shakai, Waseda UP 2006, via Kishimoto). The register wrote it in kana ひて; this is almost certainly the unvoiced register spelling of Hide, conventional kanji 秀 (to excel, outstanding), so the reading is stylized by the register's habit of dropping voicing marks. Odd-looking but genuinely recorded; commoner register style.

name: Hiru
explanation: Hiru - This name means "midday". It represents the fullness of the day, the hour when the sun stands highest and nothing is hidden, and a child expected to live openly and without shadow.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: listed by Kishimoto as an uncommon Edo commoner name that had largely vanished by Meiji; the underlying register is not named, and the name is rare, so use sparingly. Recorded in kana ひる; conventional kanji 昼 (daytime, noon), read hiru, kun reading; an everyday word as a name. Odd-looking but genuinely recorded; commoner register style.

name: Hochi
explanation: Hochi means "guarded wisdom" or "wisdom that protects", which can suggest a mind kept carefully or a knowledge used to shelter others. People with this name may be discreet, deliberate, and trusted with what must not be said aloud.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shinohara Hochi (b. 1595), early-Edo samurai woman, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 保智 (protect, keep + wisdom), on-yomi ho + chi, a conventional two-character compound. Samurai-daughter style; on-yomi two-character names of this kind were an elite register, not a village one.

name: Hangaku
explanation: Hangaku can be written with two different kanji. One means "board and tablet", and the other means "slope and tablet". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family hopes the child will stand for, such as a name carved plainly on a signboard for all to read, or one set on the hillside where a stronghold looks down on the road.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Hangaku Gozen, the Kamakura-period warrior woman of the Jo clan who held a fortress against the shogunate in 1201, on Japanese Wikipedia. Her name is written both 板額 (board + tablet or frame) and 坂額 (slope + tablet), read han-gaku, on-yomi in both; the second spelling is the one our two-kanji format uses. Warrior-family style, and famous enough that a Rokugani bearer would be read as invoking a martial heroine. Hangaku appears in ukiyo-e and in modern games as one of the archetypal onna-bugeisha.

name: Iroha
explanation: Iroha - A name that means "the first letters", evoking the opening of the syllabary that every child learns, the beginning of all learning and the promise that a life, like a poem, is written one character at a time.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Irohahime (1594-1661), eldest daughter of Date Masamune, on English Wikipedia. Her kanji are 五郎八 (five + son + eight), a boy's name chosen before her birth in expectation of a son; the reading iroha is entirely stylized, taken from the first three syllables of the iroha poem rather than from the characters (which would read Gorohachi). If used in Rokugan, explain the reading in prose or simply write it in kana. Daimyo-family style.

name: Acha
explanation: Acha chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Acha, who as a widow with no rank of her own negotiated the surrender of a besieged castle so cleanly that neither side lost face, and was granted a stipend for life.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Lady Acha (Acha no Tsubone, 1555-1637), concubine of Tokugawa Ieyasu and his envoy at the Osaka peace talks, on English Wikipedia. Kanji 阿茶 (the affectionate prefix a- + tea), read a-cha; the prefix character carries no meaning beyond endearment, so the name is essentially a pet form of Cha. Samurai or court style; the explanation's Doji Acha is a Rokugani stand-in, not canon.

name: Yamabuki
explanation: Yamabuki was a deity that was said to have covered a bare mountainside in yellow blossom after a mourning village had burned its last offering of incense, so that the dead would have flowers even when the living had none.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Yamabuki Gozen, Heian-period consort of Minamoto no Yoshinaka, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 山吹 (mountain + blow), read yama-buki, kun reading; as a compound it is the name of the kerria, the yellow spring rose, not a literal mountain wind. Court or warrior-household style in the source; flower names were also common in Edo commoner registers. Yamabuki is also the Japanese color word for that golden yellow.

name: Yonoko
explanation: Yonoko - Composed of the elements "leisure" and "open field", this name symbolizes a life with room to breathe, the child of a household that has enough and to spare. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of ease and untroubled abundance.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Udono Yonoko, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (the surname is stripped here). Kanji 余野子 (surplus, leisure + field + child), read yo-no-ko; reading is the standard one for this bearer, confirm on the article. Late-Edo elite or literate-household style; -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Yayoko
explanation: Yayoko - With origins in the legend of a shrine maiden who prayed through a failed spring until the first green shoots came up around her kneeling place, this name evokes a sense of ever-widening hope and the renewal of the world. It appeals to those who admire faith that keeps working after others have given up.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kuwabara Yayoko, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped); the source spells the given name やよ子, kana plus the -ko character. Conventional kanji 弥世子 (ever more + world, generation + child), read ya-yo-ko without strain; the kana may equally stand for 弥生 (yayoi, the third month and spring growth), which would make the reading stylized. Late-Edo literate-household style; -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Nui
explanation: Nui - Stemming from the word "sewing", which denotes the joining of cloth with needle and thread, this name embodies the spirit of mending what is torn and holding a household together seam by seam. It resonates with those who are patient, deft, and quietly indispensable.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: one of the 19 most frequent women's names (together over a quarter of 2,942 entries) in the shumon-ninbetsu-cho of Umaji village, Tanba, for 1837, 1846, 1854 and 1865 (Jugaku and Kabashima 1958, as quoted in Mori 2024). The register wrote it in kana ぬい; conventional kanji 縫 (to sew), read nui, kun reading, an everyday craft word as a name. Commoner register style at its most typical.

name: Noro
explanation: Noro - This name is inspired by the natural element of dew on an open field, symbolizing the brief brightness that comes with every dawn and is gone by the time the household is at work. It is often chosen for its connection to the morning meadow and its representation of freshness, modesty and things valued precisely because they do not last.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: listed by Kishimoto as an uncommon Edo commoner name that had largely vanished by Meiji; the underlying register is not named, and the name is rare, so use sparingly. Recorded in kana のろ; conventional kanji 野露 (field + dew), read no-ro with the on reading of 露, which is the ordinary reading in compounds. Odd-looking to a modern ear (noro also means 'slow'), but genuinely recorded; commoner register style.

name: Wiro
explanation: Wiro - A name derived from the fusion of "well" and "path", reflecting a balance between the water that stays where it is and the road that carries it to every field. It is often embraced by those who strive for a life that nourishes others without leaving home.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: cited by Kishimoto (after Tsunoda Bunei) as a name that appeared suddenly in late Edo and mostly died out without passing into Meiji; no place given, and it is rare. Recorded in kana ゐろ with the historical kana wi, so the modern reading is Iro; conventional kanji 井路 (well + road), read i-ro, a real word for an irrigation channel. Odd-looking but genuinely recorded; commoner register style.

name: Miki
explanation: Miki - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of bonsai, this name represents the trunk, the one part of the tree that every branch depends on and that the artist shapes slowest of all. It is often chosen by those who appreciate strength that is not showy and have a deep respect for cultivators who think in decades.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: cited by Kishimoto as the overwhelmingly common two-mora type across registers from Ezo to Kyushu, and also borne by named late-Edo women on Japanese Wikipedia. Registers wrote it in kana みき; conventional kanji 幹 (trunk, main stem), read miki, kun reading; modern bearers usually take 美樹 or 美紀 instead. Commoner register style, fine for any caste. Miki is a very common modern woman's name.

name: Kaku
explanation: The name Kaku is associated with the famous Flight of the Thousand Cranes, in which a river town's every household folded and released paper cranes on the same morning to mark a peace between two feuding families, and the sky over the ford went white. Those who choose this name try to embody values of reconciliation and the long life that peace makes possible.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: recorded once among the 112 women who took refuge at the Mantokuji divorce temple in Kozuke (Ueno Kazuo et al., Namae to shakai, Waseda UP 2006, via Kishimoto). The register wrote it in kana かく; the conventional kanji here is 鶴 (crane) in its on reading kaku, a sister form to the common register name Tsuru, though the kana could also stand for 覚 (awakening) or 角 (corner). Commoner register style.

name: Mon
explanation: The name Mon is inspired by the Gate of Crests in the old capital, known for the hundreds of family emblems carved into its lintels by every house that ever swore service there. The name reflects the enduring loyalty of the place and is often chosen by those who value belonging to something with a mark and a memory.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: recorded once among the 112 women who took refuge at the Mantokuji divorce temple in Kozuke (Ueno Kazuo et al., Namae to shakai, Waseda UP 2006, via Kishimoto). The register wrote it in kana もん; conventional kanji 紋 (crest, pattern), read mon, on reading and the ordinary word; 門 (gate) is the other everyday reading of the same sound. Commoner register style; very short names of this kind were normal in Edo villages.

name: Tsumaki
explanation: Tsumaki - This name pays tribute to the Hemming of the Winter Robes, a household observance at the turn of autumn that emphasizes foresight, thrift and the care a wife takes for everyone under her roof. People choose this name to reflect their values for preparation, warmth freely given and the dignity of unglamorous work.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Otsumaki, a Sengoku-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped; the source records the name in katakana ツマキ. Conventional kanji 褄 (the hem or skirt of a kimono) plus 木, or as one word 妻木 (wife + tree, also a surname), read tsuma-ki; the hem reading is the one the explanation uses, and neither spelling is attested for this bearer. Samurai-household style, though the O- form is how such women were addressed in any caste.

name: Kameju
explanation: Kameju - This name represents the long life of the tortoise and is often chosen by those who are born to a house that has lost children before, or who are expected to outlive every trouble that comes for them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shimazu Kameju (1571-1630), daughter of Shimazu Yoshihisa, on English and Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 亀寿 (tortoise + longevity), read kame-ju, a kun-on mix that was normal for elite girls' names of the period; both characters are stock auspicious elements. Daimyo-family style; the tortoise element also appears alone as Kame in Edo commoner registers.

name: Mego
explanation: Mego - This name means "love". It represents the affection a household pours into a child it has waited for, and the hope that she will be as cherished in the house she marries into as in the one that named her.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Megohime (1568-1653), wife of Date Masamune, on English and Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 愛 (love, affection); the reading mego is stylized, a Tohoku pet form of the character's kun reading (megu-mu, to cherish) rather than the ordinary ai, so a Rokugani bearer should have it explained or take a northern-dialect flavor. Daimyo-family style.

name: Tazu
explanation: Tazu means "crane of the paddies" or "the crane", which can suggest long life or the white bird that stands guard over the flooded fields at planting time. People with this name may be graceful, watchful, and slow to leave the place they were born.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Otazu no Kata, a Sengoku-period samurai woman on English and Japanese Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped. Kanji 田鶴 (paddy field + crane), read ta-zu, a classical poetic word for the crane in which the second character's reading is compressed; the reading is conventional for this word. Samurai-household style; Tazu also appears as a commoner name in Edo registers.

name: Kametsuru
explanation: Kametsuru can be written with two different kanji. One means "tortoise and crane", and the other means "tortoise and bowstring". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family most wants for a daughter, such as a life as long as the two creatures of longevity together, or one that is strong, taut and ready.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kametsuruhime (b. 1613), of a daimyo family, on Japanese Wikipedia. Her kanji are 亀鶴 (tortoise + crane), the two classic emblems of long life paired, read kame-tsuru; the alternative 亀弦 (tortoise + bowstring) in the explanation is a Rokugani spelling we supply for the two-kanji format and is not attested. Daimyo-family style; both elements also appear singly in commoner registers.

name: Minami
explanation: Minami - This name signifies the south, the direction of warmth, the noon sun and the sea road, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values openness, generosity and a face turned toward the light.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shimazu Ominami (b. 1511), a Sengoku-period samurai woman on Japanese Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped. Kanji 南 (south), read minami, kun reading; a plain direction word as a name. Samurai-household style in the source; the same plain-word pattern is common in commoner registers. Minami is a common modern given name for both sexes.

name: Tokiwa
explanation: Tokiwa - A name that means "everlasting rock", evoking the pine on the crag that keeps its green through every winter, and a constancy that outlasts the seasons.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Tokiwa Gozen (b. 1138), mother of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 常盤 (always + broad rock), read toki-wa, the classical word for something evergreen and unchanging; the reading is standard though not a simple sum of the characters' ordinary readings. Court or warrior-household style. Tokiwa Gozen is a fixture of the Heike tales and of noh and kabuki.

name: Senzuru
explanation: Senzuru chose their name in honor of the famous Kakita Senzuru, who folded a thousand paper cranes for a dying lord and then, when he recovered, folded a thousand more for the enemy who had wounded him.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Senzuru Gozen, a Heian-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 千鶴 (thousand + crane), which the modern reader would read Chizuru; sen-zuru mixes the on reading of 千 with the voiced kun reading of 鶴, a period reading that is unusual today and should count as stylized. Court or warrior-household style; the explanation's Kakita Senzuru is a Rokugani stand-in, not canon.

name: Komori
explanation: Komori was a deity that was said to have hidden a whole village of children inside a small grove of trees after a raiding army had crossed the river, so that the soldiers marched past a wood no larger than a garden and heard nothing.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Komori Gozen (d. 1189), a Heian-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 小森 (small + grove, forest), read ko-mori, kun reading, a plain landscape word that is also a common surname. Court or warrior-household style. Modern ears may hear komori as 'babysitter' (子守) or 'bat' (蝙蝠), which the explanation quietly plays on.

name: Mitsugi
explanation: Mitsugi - Derived from the phrase "the first rice goes to the lord", this name embodies the idea of tribute freely rendered, the portion that is offered before the household eats. It is often associated with those who serve without being asked and give before they are owed.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Toyota Mitsugi (1774-1829), late-Edo religious leader executed for founding a heterodox sect, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貢 (tribute, offering), read mitsugi, kun reading; a single-character word name. Commoner in origin, though the source is a Wikipedia biography rather than a village register; the character reads as commoner or merchant style.

name: Kumako
explanation: Kumako - Composed of the elements "bear" and "child", this name symbolizes a strength that protects its own, the mother bear's fierceness given to a daughter. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of hardiness, warmth, and a temper best not tested.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Ikeda Kumako, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped). Kanji 熊子 (bear + child), read kuma-ko, kun reading, straightforward. Late-Edo elite or literate-household style; animal-strength names like Kuma and Tora also appear in Edo commoner registers, and -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Tsukubako
explanation: Tsukubako - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the twin-peaked mountain that gave shelter to a wandering god when a richer mountain turned him away, in which the generous peak was blessed with visitors and green slopes forever while the proud one was cursed with snow. It reflects qualities such as hospitality, humility, and the reward of an open door.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Toki Tsukubako, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped), named for Mount Tsukuba. Kanji 筑波子 (Tsukuba, written build + wave, + child), read tsukuba-ko; the mountain name is a place name whose characters are not read for meaning, so the explanation follows the mountain's legend from the Hitachi fudoki rather than the characters. Late-Edo literate-household style; -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Koman
explanation: Koman - Rooted in the ancient proverb "a small coin kept is ten thousand earned", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value thrift, patience and the slow building of a household's fortune.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Seki no Koman (b. 1767), a late-Edo commoner woman (a teahouse keeper at the Seki post station) on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 小万 (small + ten thousand), read ko-man; Man alone was a common Edo register name and ko- is a diminutive prefix, so this is a commoner form. Commoner style; the name also belongs to several kabuki heroines, which is how most modern readers meet it.

name: Otomae
explanation: Otomae - With origins in the legend of a road-side singer who taught the songs of the common road to an Emperor's retired court until the grandest hall in the land rang with the tunes of ferrymen and packhorse drivers, this name evokes a sense of art without rank. It appeals to those who admire talent that rises from nowhere and is honored for what it is.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Otomae (1085-1169), the imayo singer who taught Emperor Go-Shirakawa, on Japanese Wikipedia; the explanation follows her real story. Kanji 乙前 (second, younger + before, front), read oto-mae, both kun readings; a name in the entertainer register, likely a stage name. Hinin or entertainer-caste style in Rokugani terms rather than court or village.

name: Kitsuno
explanation: Kitsuno - Stemming from the word "good fortune", which denotes luck that arrives as a blessing rather than a reward, this name embodies the spirit of a household touched by the Fortunes. It resonates with those who are lucky, cheerful, and generous with what came to them freely.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kitsuno (d. 1566), concubine of Oda Nobunaga and mother of Nobutada, on English Wikipedia. Kanji 吉乃 (good luck, auspicious + the particle no as a name-ender), read kitsu-no; the on reading kitsu for 吉 is conventional in names though kichi is the commoner word reading. Samurai-household style; the -no ending is also frequent in Edo commoner registers.

name: Kaji
explanation: Kaji - This name is inspired by the natural element of the paper-mulberry tree, symbolizing the leaf on which wishes are written at the Star Festival and the bark that becomes paper. It is often chosen for its connection to the riverside groves and its representation of eloquence, wishes made and words that last.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Okaji no Kata (1578-1642), concubine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, on English Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped. Kanji 梶 (paper mulberry; the same character also means an oar or rudder), read kaji, kun reading. Samurai-household style; a plain tree name of the kind commoner registers also carry. Kaji leaves are still the traditional writing surface for Tanabata wishes.

name: Onami
explanation: Onami - A name derived from the fusion of "gentle" and "south", reflecting a balance between a soft manner and the warm, sunward direction it faces. It is often embraced by those who strive for a kindness that has a definite direction and does not drift.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Onamihime (1541-1602), sister of Date Terumune and a Sengoku power in her own right, on English Wikipedia. Kanji 阿南 (the affectionate prefix 阿 + south), read o-nami, where 阿 takes the reading o rather than the usual a and 南 its ordinary kun reading; note this is on-ami, not the honorific o- on a name Nami, so the prefix is part of the name and should not be stripped. Daimyo-family style.

name: Shoju
explanation: Shoju - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of calligraphy, this name represents the auspicious character for long life brushed on the first day of the year and hung where the household will see it. It is often chosen by those who appreciate a single stroke done perfectly and have a deep respect for calligraphers whose New Year's scrolls are kept for generations.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shojuhime, a Heian-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 祥寿 (auspicious, good omen + longevity), read sho-ju, on-yomi in both, a conventional elite compound. Court style; two-character on-yomi names like this were an aristocratic register, not a village one.

name: Teruhi
explanation: The name Teruhi is associated with the famous Day of the Cleared Sky, in which a week of unbroken rain that threatened the whole rice crop broke on the morning of the Emperor's birthday and the sun shone over every province at once. Those who choose this name try to embody values of hope kept through hard weather and gratitude when it breaks.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Utsumi Teruhi, a Sengoku-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped); reading is the standard one for this bearer, confirm on the article. Kanji 照日 (to shine + sun, day), read teru-hi, both kun readings, straightforward. Samurai-household style in the source; a plain nature compound that would also sit comfortably in a commoner register.
